rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes a controlled high-temperature mechanical testing regime under plasma-facing conditions, while the paper actually used arc melting synthesis, room-temperature compression, temperature-dependent indentation plastometry, and scratch testing. This is a different kind of study (simulated service testing vs. synthesis and multi-modal mechanical characterization).
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis specifies high-temperature conditions typical for plasma-facing components with controlled heating, strain rate, and inert/vacuum atmospheres. The paper used room-temperature compression, indentation from RT to 500 °C in air, and room-temperature scratch testing. The temperature range overlaps only partially (up to 500 °C), but the specific test modes and environments differ substantially.
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis attributes enhanced plasticity and toughness to high-entropy-induced lattice distortions lowering dislocation nucleation/glide activation energy. The paper attributes strength to solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion, and plasticity/toughness to Ti, V, Zr effects on valence-electron concentration, dislocation-core modification, grain-boundary cohesion, and crack impediment. rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts increased plastic strain and improved fracture toughness under high-temperature tests. The paper predicted and observed higher strength, greater plastic strain, lower BDTT, less scratch damage, and higher fracture toughness. The direction and properties match, but the hypothesis omits strength and BDTT predictions and does not specify the magnitude of improvement.
